Article content: {"cover_media":"3_2075469699555745792","entities":{"mentions":[{"end":59,"start":46,"username":"nyk_builderz"}],"urls":[{"text":"https://github.com/0xNyk/awesome-hermes-agent"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"},{"text":"https://github.com/0xNyk/awesome-hermes-agent"},{"text":"https://t.me/+GJ-FEpzcZrtmMTky"}]},"plain_text":"Agents did not become an ecosystem because a model got smarter. They became an ecosystem the moment capabilities became installable.
That is the part of the Hermes plugin story most people are missing. The headline is "Hermes has plugins now." The real event is that agent capability just got a distribution format. And every time a platform gets a distribution format. the same thing happens. The iPhone was interesting in 2007. It became inevitable in 2008 when the App Store shipped.
I have been building on this stack for months. I maintain awesome-hermes-agent. which has crossed 14K stars mostly because people are hungry for a map of what is installable. So let me draw the map.
The first wave was chat plus tools
The first generation of agents was a model in a loop with a few tools bolted on. Call an API, run a shell command. hit a search endpoint. Powerful. but every builder wired it up from scratch. Your web-scraper was your web-scraper. My web-scraper was my web-scraper. Nothing transferred.
That is the pre-App-Store world. Lots of capability, zero distribution. If you wanted what someone else built, you read their thread and rebuilt it by hand.
The second wave is different. Plugins mean I can package a capability once, hand it to you. and you install it. The workflow. the tool bindings. the permissions. the opinionated defaults, all of it travels as one unit. That is the phase change.
The stack has more layers than people realize
Here is where the confusion lives. People use "plugin," "skill," "tool," "MCP," and "cron" as if they are the same thing. They are not, and knowing the difference is the whole game.
Layer stack:
Tool - A single capability the model can call - One call
MCP - A protocol connecting the agent to an external system - Per session
Skill - A packaged method: how to do a task well - Reused across runs
Cron - A schedule that triggers a run with no human present - Recurring
Plugin - A bundle of the above, installable and governed - Installed once, runs forever
A tool is a verb. A skill is a technique. MCP is a wire. Cron is a clock. A plugin is the box you ship all of it in.
The reason plugins are the App Store moment and not the others is that a plugin is the first unit in this stack that is both composable and governed. It bundles the tools. carries the skill. declares its permissions. and installs in one step. That is exactly what an app is.
What makes a good plugin is not what makes a good tool
When distribution shows up, the design problem changes. A good tool does one thing. A good plugin makes a decision for you.
The best plugins in the wave that is coming will not just expose capability. They will carry opinion:
A permission boundary. What this thing is and is not allowed to touch. In my own operator setup, every action routes through a content guard before it can post anything externally. A plugin that ships a capability without shipping its guardrails is a liability, not a product.
Opinionated defaults. The whole point of installing someone else's plugin is that they already made the fifty small calls you would have gotten wrong. If I have to configure everything, you gave me a tool, not a plugin.
A packaged workflow. Not "here is an API client." Instead "here is the whole job, done the way someone who does it for a living would do it."
That last one is why skills matter so much inside plugins. Anthropic's team made this argument on stage recently: do not build agents. build skills. A skill is the method. The plugin is how the method travels. Wrap a proven skill in a plugin and you have shipped expertise. not just access.
Why this is the moment, not just a feature
Every ecosystem needs three things to ignite: a way to build. a way to distribute. and a reason to trust what you install. Agents have had "build" for a while. Plugins add distribution. Governance and permission boundaries add trust.
When all three land at once, the incentive flips. Right now the smart move is to build your own everything. because there is no reliable way to consume someone else's work. The moment plugins are installable and governed. the smart move becomes: build the thing only you can build. and install the rest. That is the App Store trade. That is when the curve bends.
The takeaway
Stop thinking about whether your agent is smart enough. Start thinking about what capability you have built that only lives in your head or your repo. and whether it should be a plugin.
The first wave of agents rewarded people who could wire up tools. This wave rewards people who can package a workflow other people will install and trust. The distribution layer is here. The builders who treat their best workflows as products, not one-offs, are the ones who get compounding reach out of it.
I keep a running, curated map of the installable agent stack here: https://github.com/0xNyk/awesome-hermes-agent
What is the first agent workflow you would package as a plugin?
